answer.label: Not Richard Feynman — an anonymous modern coinage
answer.authorDates: Wording undocumented before 2014 · falsely pinned to Feynman (1918–1988)
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Richard Feynman ever said or wrote this. Quote Investigator ↗ found the Feynman-worded line only from 2014 — 26 years after his death — and traces it to an anonymous reworking of a 1995 Usenet aphorism by J. J. Hahn: “Philosophy is questions that may never be answered. Religion is answers that may never be questioned.” The exact wording has no identifiable author.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt:
“I would rather have questions that can’t be answered than answers that can’t be questioned.”

The documented ancestor, posted by J. J. Hahn in an alt.atheism signature block on 16 January 1995:
“Philosophy is questions that may never be answered. Religion is answers that may never be questioned.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ found no substantive evidence Feynman used the saying, and dates the Feynman-worded version no earlier than 2014.

The documented ancestor is J. J. Hahn’s 1995 alt.atheism signature: “Philosophy is questions that may never be answered. Religion is answers that may never be questioned” — used anonymously as an epigraph in Daniel Dennett’s 2006 Breaking the Spell ↗.
The line does not appear in the sourced section of Feynman’s Wikiquote page ↗, yet circulates widely under his name on Goodreads ↗ and social media.
source.excerptNote: The polished, Feynman-branded version is a later anonymous mutation of the 1995 aphorism; no source ties the exact wording to Feynman.

author.name: J. J. Hahn
author.heading: The documented ancestor
author.metaLine: fl. 1995 · University of Minnesota · alt.atheism Usenet poster
author.bio: J. J. Hahn is the primary documented candidate for the ancestor of this quote — not the Feynman wording itself. On 16 January 1995, Hahn posted the aphorism “Philosophy is questions that may never be answered. Religion is answers that may never be questioned” in a Usenet signature block. Quote Investigator conjectures the tidier, Feynman-branded version evolved anonymously from this line years later. Hahn may himself have been repeating something already circulating.

misattribution.heading: How Feynman’s name got attached
misattribution.intro: Richard Feynman is one of the internet’s biggest magnets for clever, skeptical-sounding lines he never uttered. This is one of them.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ found no substantive evidence Feynman ever said or wrote this. He died in 1988; the Feynman-worded line is not documented until 2014.
The nearest documented source is Hahn’s 1995 alt.atheism signature contrasting philosophy and religion — a different saying that the Feynman version appears to have been reshaped from, per QI ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: an anonymous modern coinage, popularized c. 2014, descended from a 1995 Usenet aphorism — and absent from the sourced Feynman record ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line is catnip for the way people quote Feynman: it sounds like a scientist’s creed — prizing open inquiry over dogma. But sounding like someone is not evidence they said it, and the paper trail runs the other way.

What survives scrutiny is a quieter, more interesting lineage: a 1995 Usenet signature contrasting philosophy (“questions that may never be answered”) with religion (“answers that may never be questioned”), which over two decades was compressed, symmetrized, and finally stamped with a famous name.
context.pull: Sounding like Feynman is not evidence of Feynman.
